name: Cognitive Load
description: Governs all decisions regarding cognitive load, usability, affordances, mental models, navigation conventions, error prevention, and user feedback loops. Use this skill whenever the user asks about usability, making things intuitive, reducing friction, navigation patterns, button/link design (affordances), empty states, error handling, or when evaluating how confusing a UI might be. Also trigger for any general UI/UX review task to ensure the design doesn't make the user think unnecessarily.

rules.rule: Visually differentiate interactive elements (buttons, links, inputs) from static content unequivocally.
rules.why: Users shouldn't have to hover or guess to discover what is clickable; ambiguity wastes mental energy.
rules.check: Can you tell what is clickable and what is static just by glancing at the screen?
rules.bad: A list of categories where the text is standard black without underlines or button shapes, requiring hover to reveal int
rules.good: Text links are underlined and use a distinct blue color; buttons have clear boundaries, background colors, and hover sta

rules.rule: Place standard navigation elements (logo, search, main menu, utility links) in their universally expected locations.
rules.why: Conventions reduce cognitive load because users already know how they work. Breaking them forces users to relearn basic tasks.
rules.check: Are the primary navigation and site logo exactly where the user expects them to be?
rules.bad: Hiding the main site navigation in a hamburger menu on a desktop layout to make the design look "cleaner".
rules.good: The logo is in the top left, primary navigation runs horizontally across the top, and utility links (login/cart) are top

rules.rule: Prioritize the ease of the clicks (scent of information) over the absolute number of clicks. Three easy, thoughtless clicks are better than one agonizing click.
rules.why: Users don't mind clicking if each click clearly advances them toward their goal and requires no thought.
rules.check: Is the user certain they are moving in the right direction before they click?
rules.bad: A mega-menu that requires the user to carefully parse 50 options just to reach a page in one click.
rules.good: A clear, 3-step wizard where each step asks a single, obvious question.

rules.rule: Place the most likely desired option early in the scan path so users can find it without reading every option.
rules.why: Users don't weigh all options to find the best one; they pick the first one that seems "good enough."
rules.check: Is the most common choice positioned so it is seen first?
rules.bad: An alphabetical list of countries in a dropdown where "United States" is buried at the bottom despite being the choice f
rules.good: A country dropdown that pins the top 3 most common countries to the very top of the list.

rules.rule: Use visual hierarchies, bold text, bulleted lists, and short paragraphs to make text highly scannable.
rules.why: Users scan pages looking for keywords relevant to their goal; dense text blocks block scanning.
rules.check: Can you extract the main points of the page by only reading the headings and bolded text?
rules.bad: A feature description is written as a single, dense 400-word paragraph.
rules.good: The feature is broken down into three bullet points with bolded keywords.

rules.rule: Cut the word count of instructional text in half, then cut it in half again. Remove "happy talk" entirely.
rules.why: Extraneous text dilutes the useful information, forcing the user to work harder to find what matters.
rules.check: Does every word on the screen directly help the user understand the interface or accomplish their task?
rules.bad: "Welcome to our platform! We've worked hard to bring you these features. Please click the button below to get started wi
rules.good: "Create your account."

rules.rule: Reveal advanced or secondary features only when the user specifically requests them.
rules.why: Showing every possible option upfront overwhelms the user and clutters the interface.
rules.check: Are you showing options that less than 20% of users will need by default?
rules.bad: A search form that shows 15 advanced filtering criteria immediately upon loading.
rules.good: A search form with a single text input and an "Advanced Filters" toggle that expands the remaining options.

rules.rule: Display available options or required formats rather than forcing the user to remember them.
rules.why: The human brain is much better at recognizing something it sees than recalling it from memory.
rules.check: Does the user have to rely on their memory from a previous step to complete this step?
rules.bad: An API key field that asks the user to type their key without providing a link or dropdown to select existing keys.
rules.good: An input field that shows a dropdown of recently used API keys for immediate selection.

rules.rule: Design interfaces so that incorrect actions are impossible to make (forcing functions).
rules.why: Preventing an error is infinitely better than providing a great error message after the fact.
rules.check: Is it physically possible for the user to submit invalid data?
rules.bad: A text input for a date that allows the user to type "February 30th", returning an error upon submission.
rules.good: A date picker UI that greys out invalid dates, making them unselectable.

rules.rule: Every user action must result in immediate visual or auditory feedback indicating the system received the input.
rules.why: Without feedback, users assume the system is broken or the action failed, often leading them to repeat the action.
rules.check: Does the interface react within 100ms when the user interacts with it?
rules.bad: Clicking "Submit" on a form does nothing visually until the next page loads 3 seconds later.
rules.good: Clicking "Submit" immediately disables the button and changes its label to "Saving..." alongside a spinner.

rules.rule: Ensure the spatial layout of controls directly maps to the spatial arrangement of the elements they affect.
rules.why: Natural mapping leverages physical analogies, making the interface instantly intuitive without instructions.
rules.check: If there are multiple controls, does their layout mirror the layout of the things they control?
rules.bad: A row of four identical switches to control four different lights, requiring labels to differentiate them.
rules.good: A volume slider where moving the thumb UP increases the volume and DOWN decreases it.

rules.rule: Ensure every affordance (what an element *can* do) has a visible signifier (a cue telling the user *how* to do it).
rules.why: An invisible affordance is useless; users must know an action is possible before they can perform it.
rules.check: Does the element visually communicate how it should be interacted with?
rules.bad: A card component that is entirely clickable but lacks hover states, an arrow icon, or button styling.
rules.good: A draggable list item that displays a "grip" icon (six dots) to signify it can be grabbed and moved.

rules.rule: Make the sequence of actions required to achieve a goal explicit and visible.
rules.why: Users struggle when they know their goal but cannot figure out which buttons to press to achieve it.
rules.check: Does the user know exactly what to do next to progress toward their goal?
rules.bad: A complex settings page where the "Save" button is hidden inside a separate tab.
rules.good: A multi-step checkout process with a clear progress bar and an obvious "Continue" button at the bottom of each step.

rules.rule: Provide clear, plain-language confirmation that an action successfully achieved the user's intent.
rules.why: Users need to know not just that a button was clicked, but that the *system state* has changed as desired.
rules.check: After taking an action, is the user absolutely certain of the new system state?
rules.bad: A generic "Success!" toast message after updating a profile, without showing the updated profile.
rules.good: A toast message saying "Email address updated to user@example.com" and instantly reflecting the change in the UI.

rules.rule: Design the interface based on how the user *thinks* the system works, not how the underlying engineering actually works.
rules.why: Exposing the system's implementation model confuses users who lack the technical context.
rules.check: Does the interface use terminology and structures that a non-expert understands?
rules.bad: An error message that says "Database constraint violation: duplicate entry on key 'email_idx'".
rules.good: An error message that says "An account with this email address already exists."

rules.rule: Ensure that content extending below the fold provides a visual cue (a "cut-off" element) indicating there is more to see.
rules.why: If a layout perfectly aligns with the bottom edge of the screen, users may assume they've reached the end and stop scrolling.
rules.check: Does the layout clearly look like it continues beyond the visible screen edge?
rules.bad: A grid of cards where exactly two rows fit perfectly on screen, leaving no partial cards visible at the bottom.
rules.good: A list where the bottom-most item is cut in half by the edge of the screen, inviting the user to scroll.

rules.rule: Always provide an obvious way to cancel an action, go back, or return to the home page.
rules.why: Users make mistakes and explore dead ends; feeling trapped breeds anxiety and frustration.
rules.check: Can the user easily back out of their current screen or workflow without using the browser's back button?
rules.bad: A modal dialog that has no "X" button and no "Cancel" button, forcing the user to commit.
rules.good: A multi-step form that includes a "Cancel" link next to the primary action on every step.

rules.rule: When errors do occur, explain exactly what went wrong and provide a direct path to fix it.
rules.why: Blaming the user or providing dead-end errors destroys trust. The cost of an error is the time it takes to recover from it.
rules.check: Does the error message tell the user exactly what to do to fix the problem?
rules.bad: A form submission fails with the message "Invalid data" and clears all the user's inputs.
rules.good: The form preserves the user's inputs, highlights the exact field that failed, and explains the required format.

rules.rule: Visually separate utility navigation (login, help, settings) from primary content navigation.
rules.why: Mixing tools with content confuses the user's mental map of the site's structure.
rules.check: Are utility links visually distinct and positioned separately from the main navigational categories?
rules.bad: Placing "Help" and "Sign Out" in the exact same styling and visual list as "Products" and "Services".
rules.good: Primary navigation is large and centered, while utility links are smaller and pushed to the top right corner.

rules.rule: Apply a single, consistent visual treatment to all text links across the entire interface.
rules.why: Making links look different on different pages breaks the user's learned recognition, forcing them to re-evaluate what is clickable.
rules.check: Are all text links instantly recognizable by a consistent color or underline?
rules.bad: Using blue links in the sidebar, green links in the footer, and red links in the body text.
rules.good: Using a specific shade of blue and an underline for all inline text links globally.  ## Anti-patterns  ### The Memory Ta
